transfer.stem: Which summary keeps the report, interview question and sign accurate?
transfer.passage:
Preparing a nature-park report
Our class used a magazine that included a guide to local wildlife. This did not mean that the guide was its only feature or that it listed every animal. An article explained why a river floods; we did not use it to predict the exact date of another flood.
Our report separated facts from opinions. We wanted readers to distinguish checkable statements from personal judgements, although we still had to verify our information. Before a possible interview with a park volunteer, we prepared open questions. For example, “How do you help protect local wildlife?” invited an explanation. “Do you work here?” mainly invited yes or no. The picture was a writing setting, not evidence that an interview had already taken place.
We needed accurate information about the route. Needing it did not mean that every detail had already been checked. Clear communication could prevent many small mistakes, but it could not guarantee that nobody would ever make a mistake.
We also read an instruction to raise a hand as a signal to stop. It did not say that everyone had stopped. A sign warned drivers about a narrow bridge, but this account gave no weight limit or exact width.

options.text: The report treated opinions as facts; the interview question invited an explanation; the sign warned of a narrow bridge.
The report separated facts from opinions; the interview question invited only yes or no; the sign warned of a narrow bridge.
The report separated facts from opinions; the interview question invited an explanation; the account gave the exact bridge weight limit.
The report separated facts from opinions; the interview question invited an explanation; the sign warned of a narrow bridge.
